title: Jesus of Nazareth
summary: Jewish teacher from Galilee, baptized by John and crucified in Jerusalem under the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate; the movement that formed around him became Christianity. Birth year and exact date of death are debated.
card: Jesus was a Jewish man from Nazareth in Galilee who was baptized by John in the Jordan and executed by crucifixion in Jerusalem while Pontius Pilate governed Judaea. Two Roman-era writers, Josephus and Tacitus, mention him or his execution, and nearly all historians accept that he lived. His birth lies somewhere around 6 to 1 BCE and his death between 30 and 33 CE, and the miraculous and resurrection claims are matters of Christian belief rather than historical finding.
what: Jesus (Aramaic and Hebrew Yeshua) was a Jewish man from Nazareth, a village in Galilee, in the Roman-dominated Herodian lands of the early first century CE. The Gospels of Matthew and Luke place his birth in Bethlehem during the reign of Herod the Great, while Mark and Luke show him growing up in Nazareth and working there, and Mark names a mother, Mary, and brothers called James, Joses, Judas and Simon. Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's preaching to the fifteenth year of Tiberius (28 or 29 CE) and says Jesus, then about thirty, was baptized by John in the Jordan. Jesus then taught and gathered followers, and the Gospels describe healings and exorcisms that Christians understand as miracles. The Gospels agree that he was brought to Pontius Pilate, who governed Judaea as prefect from about 26 to 36 CE, and was crucified at Golgotha in Jerusalem, with women among those who watched and a member of the council burying him in a rock-cut tomb. Christians believe he rose from the dead on the third day; this is a claim of faith that historians neither confirm nor refute. Outside the Christian texts, Josephus twice mentions him, the second time by naming James as his brother, and Tacitus says that the Christians took their name from Christus, executed under Tiberius by Pilate. Most scholars treat the baptism and the crucifixion as the best-established facts. Several details remain disputed: the birth year, because Herod's death is placed anywhere from about 5 to 1 BCE; the year of the crucifixion, usually given as 30 or 33 CE; and how much of Josephus's longer passage is original. The idea that Jesus never lived is held by a small minority and rejected by the great majority of historians.

uncertainty.note: Birth is placed before the death of Herod the Great, which the majority dates to 4 BCE (birth c. 6-5 BCE) but which scholars have argued for as late as 1 BCE; the start year -4 is 5 BCE. Death is placed in the tenure of Pilate (26-36 CE), most often 30 or 33 CE; 30 is used as the earlier of the two.

how: The surviving evidence comes in two layers. The Christian layer is the four Gospels and other New Testament writings, which are shaped by belief but preserve details that scholars use: a Galilean home, a baptism by John, a family with named brothers, a trial before Pilate and a Jerusalem crucifixion. The outside layer is Josephus and Tacitus. Josephus describes Pilate's governorship and, in the Testimonium Flavianum, a Jesus condemned by Pilate; the manuscripts are medieval and many scholars think Christian copyists reworked the wording, though most think a core is Josephan, and a later short notice calls James the brother of the one called Christ. Tacitus reports the execution under Tiberius when explaining why Nero blamed Christians for the fire of Rome. Dating relies on synchronisms: Luke's fifteenth year of Tiberius for the start of the ministry, Pilate's governorship of about 26 to 36 CE for the death, and the death of Herod the Great as the latest limit for the birth. The Pilate inscription from Caesarea confirms Pilate's existence and his title of prefect.
why_it_matters: The life, death and reported resurrection of Jesus gave rise to Christianity, a world religion that has shaped art, law, learning and politics wherever it has spread. The BCE/CE year numbering conventionally takes his birth as its anchor, so dates throughout this Atlas are expressed against him, even though his actual birth year is uncertain. A concrete consequence of the movement is visible within one lifetime of his death: Tacitus records that by the 60s CE his followers had reached Rome and were blamed by Nero for a fire, the start of a long history of persecution. Without a crucifixion under a Roman governor, and without followers who held that he had been raised, a Galilean teacher would probably be known, if at all, only as a footnote; the name Christians, and the Church that bears it, would not exist in anything like their form. Questions of faith are left to the traditions concerned; the historical record here covers what the evidence supports.

perspectives.holder: Majority of historians (reign of Herod ending 4 BCE)
perspectives.account: Herod died in the spring of 4 BCE after a lunar eclipse and before Passover, so Jesus was born in about 6 to 5 BCE; this view dates back to Emil Schürer.

perspectives.holder: Kushnir-Stein and other revisionists (death in winter 4/3 BCE or earlier)
perspectives.account: Josephus's evidence fits a death in winter 4/3 BCE equally well, and some alternatives place it in November or December of 5 BCE, which would move the birth slightly earlier.

perspectives.holder: Steinmann and W. E. Filmer (death in early 1 BCE)
perspectives.account: Herod reigned from late 39 BCE to early 1 BCE; Jesus would then have been about 31 to 33 years old in 29 CE, a fit with Luke.

perspectives.holder: Colin J. Humphreys and W. G. Waddington (1983)
perspectives.account: Astronomical calculations of the Jewish calendar and a lunar eclipse recorded on Passover point to Friday 3 April 33 CE as the date of the crucifixion.

perspectives.holder: Scholars who think the Testimonium Flavianum was reworked by Christian copyists
perspectives.account: Josephus wrote something about Jesus, but wording such as the statement that he was the Christ and had risen was added by later scribes; the earliest manuscripts are medieval.
The passage may not have been edited as heavily as assumed, based on how early translators and Christian writers read it and on who might have informed Josephus.

perspectives.holder: Mythicists (minority) and critics such as Edmund Standing
perspectives.account: Mythicists hold that the Gospels refer to no real person; Standing argues the opposite, that the apocalyptic expectations attached to Jesus point to a historical preacher.

perspectives.holder: Philosophical and historical analysis of miracle and resurrection claims
perspectives.account: Historians and philosophers distinguish between historical events open to empirical verification and claims of miraculous resurrection, which represent theological commitments and matters of faith.
